transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-04-28 12:00 PM ET
- Duration: 47 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Anita Patel (Redwood Solutions); Rajiv Malhotra (CTO), Lena Ortiz (Head of ML), Samir Khan (Procurement), Priya Singh (Eng Mgr)

Auto-generated summary (brief):
Veridian evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private/VPC. Primary driver: reduce generation costs for clinical summarization workflows while meeting security/compliance constraints (PHI considerations). Wants clear per-token unit economics, impact of batching/caching/quantization, and a pilot plan to validate latency and cost targets.

Topics covered:
- Current stack and usage pattern
- Per-token hosted pricing and volume tiers
- Dedicated capacity economics and amortization
- Batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization trade-offs
- VPC/private deployment constraints (KMS, audit logs, SOC2)
- Benchmarks and pilot next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — uh— I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Carlos, our SE, Anita is on to help with commercial questions. How's everyone?
[00:12] Rajiv Malhotra: Good, thanks. We wanted to dig into cost. We run a clinical summarization microservice, lots of short context calls and some longer discharge summaries. Our concern is per-call cost and also regulatory — PHI.
[00:25] Carlos Rivera: Great. Can you give a sense of QPS and average token lengths? Rough numbers are fine.
[00:32] Lena Ortiz: Sure— most calls are 150 to 600 tokens, average around 320. Peak QPS ~8, steady 3–4. We expect growth. Also few very long jobs for multi-page notes, like 3k tokens, but rare.
[00:45] Maya Chen: Helpful. On pricing, we typically show hosted per-token tiers, dedicated reserved capacity amortized monthly, and private/VPC which has platform fees. For cost comparison I want to run some worked examples with your token distributions.
[00:56] Samir Khan: Two constraints: 1) procurement wants a clear TCO year 1 and year 2, 2) compliance needs to understand how keys and logs are handled for PHI.
[01:08] Carlos Rivera: Noted. Quick note on levers: batching, prefix/KV caching, and quantization. For short calls batching can be tricky because latency SLOs matter, but prefix caching often helps if you have repeated templates or shared context. Quantization reduces GPU memory and can lower per-token cost if model quality stays acceptable.
[01:28] Priya Singh: Could you quantify "lower per-token cost"? Like percent ranges for our workload?
[01:35] Carlos Rivera: Rough ballpark — if you move from naive hosted (no caching/batching) to optimized hosted with caching + small batch windows, you might see 15–30% reduction. Dedicated with good packing and quantized model could be another 20–40% lower at scale, but depends on utilization. So total possible delta 30–60% between naive hosted vs optimized dedicated for some workloads. Those are very approximate.
[01:58] Rajiv Malhotra: That's a wide range; we need concrete numbers. Also can you explain amortization on dedicated — how do we think about committed GPUs vs burst?
[02:07] Maya Chen: Yeah, for dedicated we present an amortized per-token that takes committed monthly cost, estimated utilization, and average throughput (tokens/sec) into account. If you commit to a pool and reach high utilization, unit cost drops — but the commit is a fixed monthly cost. We also have burst options for short spikes.
[02:22] Lena Ortiz: How do you handle KV cache for multi-turn notes? We have repeated boilerplate sections.
[02:28] Carlos Rivera: For multi-turn or repeated boilerplate, prefix caching stores token keys (KV cache) so we avoid recomputation on the same prefixes. That helps especially with templates — saves decode compute. It works both in hosted and dedicated. In dedicated you can tune cache retention and the cluster will keep hot keys in memory.
[02:46] Rajiv Malhotra: Any quantization support? We're sensitive to accuracy for clinical text.
[02:51] Carlos Rivera: We support multiple quantization profiles — 4-bit, 8-bit, and mixed. We recommend running a quality eval set — Redwood Optimize can suggest a profile that balances cost and fidelity. For clinical, we usually start with 8-bit or mixed and run an eval harness.
[03:10] Samir Khan: On compliance: KMS integration, customer-managed keys, and audit logs — how mature is that in private deployment vs hosted?
[03:17] Anita Patel: Good question. Hosted supports envelope encryption and managed KMS; we also offer Bring-Your-Own-Key for certain tiers. Dedicated gives stronger isolation and we can integrate with your KMS for keys at rest; Private/VPC lets you control the control plane and connect HSMs in on-prem scenarios. We have SOC2 and ISO docs we can share.
[03:36] Lena Ortiz: Do you have any documented PII/PHI handling for logs? We need retention controls and redaction.
[03:43] Maya Chen: Yes — we can provide our security pack. For private deployments, you can opt out of log retention or forward logs to your own S3. We'll include those docs in the follow-up.
[03:52] Priya Singh: Back to economics — can you give a worked example? Say 1M calls/month, avg 320 tokens.
[03:59] Carlos Rivera: Quick math— 1M calls * 320 tokens = 320M tokens. For hosted, our public list price on the model bench is X per 1k tokens — (note: redacted on call). For an example, if hosted list is $0.002 per 1k tokens (hypothetical), that'd be $640. But real list is higher; let me do a scenario with three tiers — naive hosted, optimized hosted, and dedicated.
[04:28] Maya Chen: I'll flag that the exact numbers in our pricing sheet will replace placeholders. The important thing is modeling: tokens, compression from caching, effective batching throughput, and commit amortization.
[04:40] Rajiv Malhotra: How does caching reduce that 320M effective tokens?
[04:44] Carlos Rivera: If 30% of your calls contain repeated templates and the cache hits 60% of those prefixes, your decode compute for those parts is avoided. So you might reduce net decode tokens by, say, 10–15% in this example. Also batching aggregates requests so you can fill GPU steps more efficiently — which helps dedicated the most.
[05:05] Lena Ortiz: In the long-run if our usage triples, do you recommend dedicated or private?
[05:10] Maya Chen: For growth trajectories and strict compliance, many customers start with hosted to validate quality and prompts, then move to dedicated when predictable throughput and cost matter, and consider private/VPC when they need customer-managed control and full audit trail. But there's no single path — we can do hybrid routing to keep fallbacks.
[05:28] Samir Khan: Procurement question — what terms for overage and commit?
[05:31] Anita Patel: We typically offer monthly reserved capacity with a 12 or 36 month commitment; overage rates apply based on pre-agreed thresholds. We'll include a template in the follow-up.
[05:42] (Brief cross-talk)
[06:00] Carlos Rivera: One more point — routing policies. You can route latency-sensitive short calls to a lower-cost hosted model variant or to dedicated based on SLO. That gives cost flexibility.
[06:14] Priya Singh: Do you support A/B routing to test quantized model vs full-precise model?
[06:18] Carlos Rivera: Yes, rollouts and A/B is part of the console. You can split traffic, measure quality regressions, and auto-fallback if quality drops. Useful for clinical evaluation.
[06:31] Rajiv Malhotra: How long would a pilot take to prove unit economics?
[06:35] Maya Chen: From our experience: a 2–4 week pilot with representative traffic and your eval set gives good signals. If we do hosted vs dedicated bench, add another week for provisioning and metrics. So plan 3–5 weeks end-to-end.
[06:48] Lena Ortiz: For the pilot, what metrics will you measure?
[06:52] Carlos Rivera: Latency P50/P95/P99, throughput, per-token cost, GPU utilization, cache hit ratio, and quality metrics from your eval harness (ROC/precision, or clinician annotations). We'll provide the dashboard template.
[07:06] Samir Khan: On the financial side — we need a year 1, year 2 TCO comparing hosted consumption vs a 12-month dedicated commit. Will you run a scenario?
[07:14] Maya Chen: Yes— we'll run 3 scenarios: conservative (lower growth), expected, and high growth. We'll include amortized cost, projected utilization, and break-even points.
[07:24] Priya Singh: What about model selection? If we pick a smaller model to save cost, quality might suffer. How do you help pick?
[07:29] Carlos Rivera: Redwood Optimize can recommend model variants and quantization settings for your workload. We also run evals against your prompt sets to surface quality deltas.
[07:39] Rajiv Malhotra: Competitors — we talked to OpenAI already for hosted pricing and Vertex AI for managed endpoints. Any differentiators you want to highlight?
[07:46] Maya Chen: We position on production-grade inference and economics transparency — clear unit-econ levers (batching/caching/quantization/routing), and consistent tooling across hosted/dedicated/private. Also the rollouts and eval integration for quality gating.
[07:58] Lena Ortiz: A little nit — how much engineering work to switch from hosted to dedicated?
[08:02] Carlos Rivera: We aim for minimal app changes— same API and client. For VPC/private there is more network configuration and key setup. For dedicated, you may need to tune batch windows and concurrency but the interface remains the same.
[08:16] Samir Khan: For procurement timeline, we might need a draft SOW and MSAs. Can you share standard contracts?
[08:20] Anita Patel: Yes, procurement — we'll share the MSA + SOW templates. We'll also include security addenda.
[08:27] (Pause)
[08:40] Lena Ortiz: Quick technical question — when you say "pack GPUs" for dedicated, what does that mean operationally?
[08:44] Carlos Rivera: Means we schedule many small requests onto the same GPU by batching and packing sequences of different lengths to maximize throughput. That lowers per-token compute idle time. We also use continuous batching windows and kernel selection to optimize long vs short sequences.
[09:01] Rajiv Malhotra: Can we get a sample spreadsheet with amortization math?
[09:05] Maya Chen: Absolutely — that's the first attachment we'll send.
[09:09] Priya Singh: Any red flags for clinical workloads? Latency SLOs and hallucination risk — do you have guardrails?
[09:16] Carlos Rivera: For hallucination, we recommend prompt engineering and reranking or grounding strategies; Redwood supports function-calling and tool integration to augment outputs. For strict SLOs, dedicate pools and regional routing help reduce variance.
[09:30] Maya Chen: Before we wrap, quick recap of next steps and owners. I'll send pricing scenarios + amortization spreadsheet; Carlos will send benchmarking plan and script; Lena will send prompt/eval set; Samir will share procurement templates.
[09:44] Rajiv Malhotra: Good. Also can you include a cost sensitivity analysis that shows break-even at different utilization levels?
[09:50] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll include break-even curves.
[09:53] (Silence)
[10:00] End of recorded excerpt.
